Each track has a card: the question it asks, where its records come from, what drives each sound, what is simulated rather than observed, what to be careful about, and how to reproduce it byte for byte. A track's version changes when its music changes; the changelog says when and why. Tracks are grouped into albums. See [Methods](methods.qmd#versions-variants-and-remixes) for how versions, variants and remixes work, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` to propose a remix.

# Water Year Rings

One hydrologic year in two southern British Columbia watersheds, on recorded acoustic instruments. [The album's page](water-year.qmd).

## Granby River, water year 2024 {#granby-wy2024}

**v1.0** · WY2024 (water year, 2023-10-01 to 2024-09-30) · [listen](listen.qmd?piece=granby_wy2024)

*What does a warm El Niño winter sound like on a small mountain river: a year that never fully committed to winter, with broken ice and an early, small freshet?*

**Place.** The Granby River at Grand Forks and its tributary Burrell Creek, with the Billings climate station, in the Kettle River basin of southern British Columbia.

**Records.**

- Granby River at Grand Forks, daily discharge and ice flag (Water Survey of Canada 08NN002)
- Burrell Creek above Gloucester Creek, daily discharge (WSC 08NN023)
- Billings daily climate (ECCC station 1100)
- Plant productivity (NASA MODIS MOD17A2HGF, Granby valley point)

| Record | What you hear | |
|---|---|---|
| Granby River flow | Piano gets denser as flow rises; contrabass holds the root, cello adds a 5th at high flow. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Flow vs. 15-yr normal | Sets the harmony's brightness: below normal leans one mode darker, above normal one brighter. | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| Burrell Creek flow | Hand drums: tumba, conga, shaker, and a 3-3-2 log-drum figure at the peak. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Ice conditions (WSC flag) | Freeze: falling glockenspiel + bowed cymbal. Frozen: crackle and descending singing-ice chirps. Breakup: cymbal swell and rising harp. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Air temperature, Billings | Colder days make the ice crackle denser; also brightens the harmony across the season. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Rain | Each rainy day scatters harp notes from the current chord. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Snowfall | Snowfall scatters soft glockenspiel notes, high up. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Snow on ground | Deep snow swaps the reverb to a dark, short room: snow absorbs sound. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Plant productivity (MODIS GPP) | Violins swell with photosynthesis. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Redband trout spawning | A short rising flute figure. Timing is modelled from temperature and season. | <span class="src S">S</span> |
| Mountain whitefish spawning | A falling cello pizzicato figure. Timing is modelled. | <span class="src S">S</span> |
| Day length | With temperature, sets how bright the mode is. | <span class="src D">D</span> |

Every step from record to sound, with its bounds: [the mapping dictionary](dictionary/granby-wy2024-mapping.html) (tables in `tracks/mapping/granby-wy2024/`).

**Harmony.** Key of D, 72 bpm, one bar per three days (122 bars, about 7 minutes). The mode moves along a dark-to-bright ladder, from Aeolian to Ionian, set by day length and temperature, and nudged one step by how the river's flow compares with its 2010-24 normal; it changes at most one step every eight bars. The river's phase (dormant, rising, peak, recession, low) chooses a four-chord loop.

**Simulated, not observed.**

- Redband trout and mountain whitefish spawning windows, modelled from air temperature and season.
- Bird arrival windows (dipper, Swainson's thrush, bank swallow), typical regional timing, not sightings.

**Be careful about.**

- Air temperature stands in for water temperature; no Granby stream-temperature record was available.
- The ice record is WSC's "Ice Conditions" data flag, which marks when ice affected the gauge, not an observation of the whole river.
- Plant productivity is the mean of a 2.3 km block and mixes land covers.

**Reproduce.** `python scripts/pilot_granby_wy2024.py` · seed 2024 · locked 2026-09-27 · SHA-256 of the MP3 on this site `d047773665713d75…` · check it with `python scripts/renders.py verify granby-wy2024`

**Credits.** Graham Watt, the question, the rivers and records, listening and direction; Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding agent), music theory, mapping and all of the code; Instruments, VSCO 2 Community Edition (Versilian Studios, CC0); birds from Wikimedia Commons (see samples_manifest.csv).

**Lineage.** variants: `frozen`, `no-perc`, `slow`.

**Changelog.**

- v1.0 (2026-09-25): First published version.

## Okanagan, water year 2024 {#okanagan-wy2024}

**v1.0** · WY2024 (water year, 2023-10-01 to 2024-09-30) · [listen](listen.qmd?piece=okanagan_wy2024)

*What does it sound like when a drought year on a regulated lake is also the biggest sockeye return in a decade?*

**Place.** Okanagan Lake at Kelowna and the Okanagan River at Penticton and near Oliver, with the Summerland climate station, in southern British Columbia; and Wells Dam on the Columbia, below the Okanagan confluence.

**Records.**

- Okanagan Lake at Kelowna, daily level (WSC 08NM083)
- Okanagan River at Penticton, dam outflow (WSC 08NM050)
- Okanagan River near Oliver, daily discharge (WSC 08NM085)
- Summerland CS daily climate (ECCC station 979)
- Plant productivity (NASA MODIS MOD17A2HGF, Summerland point)
- Adult sockeye and water temperature at Wells Dam (Columbia River DART; fetched, not redistributed)

| Record | What you hear | |
|---|---|---|
| Okanagan Lake level, Kelowna | A low F held under everything, louder as the lake fills; cello adds a 5th while it rises. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Lake vs. 15-yr normal | Sets the harmony's brightness: below normal leans one mode darker. | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| Outflow at Penticton dam | Piano density follows the release. When the dam holds the flow flat, the piano plays strictly, with no variation. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Okanagan River near Oliver | Soft log drums, conga and shaker. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Sockeye passing Wells Dam | Marimba runs climb the chord; more fish means more notes, and the runs start higher as the season goes. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Water temperature at Wells | Above 18 C a violin holds a high note: thermal stress for migrating sockeye. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Sockeye spawning near Oliver | Low, falling cello pizzicato around mid-October, scaled by run size. Timing is modelled. | <span class="src S">S</span> |
| Air temperature, Summerland | Below -8 C: frost crackle. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Rain | Harp notes from the current chord. Rain vs. snow is split by temperature. | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| Snow | Soft, high glockenspiel. | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| Humidity (daily min) | Humid days get a long hall reverb; dry days a short, bright room. | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Plant productivity (MODIS GPP) | Violins swell with photosynthesis. | <span class="src R">R</span> |

Every step from record to sound, with its bounds: [the mapping dictionary](dictionary/okanagan-wy2024-mapping.html) (tables in `tracks/mapping/okanagan-wy2024/`).

**Harmony.** Key of F, 64 bpm, one bar per three days (122 bars, about 8 minutes). The same mode ladder as the Granby piece, set by day length and temperature and nudged by the lake's level against its 2010-24 normal. The lake's phase (winter, filling, full, drawdown) chooses the chord loop, and the piano plays strictly, without variation, while the dam holds the outflow flat.

**Simulated, not observed.**

- Sockeye spawning near Oliver, timing modelled around mid-October and scaled by the run that produced it.
- Bird arrival windows (western meadowlark, sandhill crane), typical timing, not sightings.

**Be careful about.**

- The Wells temperature is Columbia River water, pumped from the dam tailrace into the fishway, not Okanagan water.
- Summerland's separate rain and snow values are missing on most days, so rain and snow are split from total precipitation by temperature (derived).
- Lake level is measured from the gauge's local datum, not sea level.

**Reproduce.** `python scripts/pilot_okanagan_wy2024.py` · seed 1997 · locked 2026-09-27 · SHA-256 of the MP3 on this site `f2c2e997c5c33d64…` · check it with `python scripts/renders.py verify okanagan-wy2024`

**Credits.** Graham Watt, the question, the rivers and records, listening and direction; Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding agent), music theory, mapping and all of the code; Instruments, VSCO 2 Community Edition (Versilian Studios, CC0); birds from Wikimedia Commons (see samples_manifest.csv).

# Climate Pair

Sixty-eight years of the global climate record, one year per bar, heard from the Pacific and from the Atlantic. [The album's page](climate.qmd).

## Climate Pair: Pacific {#climate-pair-pacific}

**v2.0** · 1958-2025 (calendar years, 1958-01-01 to 2025-12-31) · [listen](climate.qmd?piece=pacific)

*Can seventy years of a warming planet be heard as one rising form, with the ocean's own cycles and storms moving through it?*

**Place.** The global record, heard from the Pacific: its ocean phase and storms, and the Kettle River, which crosses the BC-Washington border near Grand Forks.

**Records.**

- Mauna Loa CO₂ (NOAA GML)
- Global ocean surface temperature anomaly (NOAA NCEI) and global temperature (NASA GISTEMP v4)
- Ocean heat content 0-2000 m (IAP v4.2; fetched, not redistributed)
- Oceanic Niño Index (NOAA CPC)
- Kettle River near Laurier, annual peak daily flow (USGS 12404500)
- Pacific Decadal Oscillation (NOAA NCEI)
- West Pacific (IBTrACS) and Northeast and Central Pacific (HURDAT2) best tracks
- Sunspot number (SILSO; fetched, not redistributed)

| Layer | Data | What you hear | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Drone and organ pedal | Mauna Loa CO₂, deseasonalized (NOAA GML) | level and brightness rise with ppm; the seasonal CO₂ cycle makes it breathe | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Cellos | global ocean surface temperature anomaly (NOAA NCEI) | chord tones, from one voice to three, louder as it warms | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Contrabass | ocean heat content, 0-2000 m (IAP v4.2) | the deep ocean filling: root, then root and fifth, louder | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Chords and month pulse | Oceanic Niño Index (NOAA CPC) | El Niño lifts the chords, La Niña sinks them; one pulse note a month, louder in strong years | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Mode and pad | Pacific Decadal Oscillation, 3-year mean | Dorian in the warm phase, Aeolian in the cool; the pad brightens with the index | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| Drums | West Pacific typhoons (IBTrACS, panned left) and Northeast Pacific hurricanes (HURDAT2, panned right) | tropical storm: bass-drum rub; hurricane: timpani; major: timpani, bass drum and sub; category 5: tam-tam; landfall: cymbal | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Rumble | season's accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) | a low storm rumble | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| Shimmer | sunspot number (SILSO) | high shimmer and glockenspiel sparkles on the 11-year cycle | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| High violin | global temperature anomaly (NASA GISTEMP) | a held high note once it passes +0.8 °C | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Gong | large volcanic eruptions and their cooling | a gong; the drone darkens for about two years | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| Harp bloom | Kettle River annual peak flow (USGS 12404500) | a spring harp and piano bloom, sized by the peak's rank | <span class="src R">R</span> |

Every step from record to sound, with its bounds: [the mapping dictionary](dictionary/climate-pair-pacific-mapping.html) (tables in `tracks/mapping/climate-pair-pacific/`).

**Harmony.** Key of D, one bar per year (68 bars of 7 seconds, about 8 minutes); the four beats are the seasons and the twelve pulses the months. ENSO sets the chords and the ocean's multidecadal phase sets the mode.

**Be careful about.**

- Early storms are undercounted, before routine satellite coverage (about 1966; later in the Northeast Pacific).
- Records end at different times. Interior gaps are interpolated and each record's last value is held to the end.
- The ocean phases are 3-year means, so their turns sound about two years late.
- The volcanic cooling shape, the ENSO-to-chord table and every loudness curve are interpretive choices, not measurements.

**Reproduce.** `python scripts/climate_pair.py pacific` · seeds 1958, 99 · locked 2026-09-27 · SHA-256 of the MP3 on this site `314128ee9c53d2ad…` · check it with `python scripts/renders.py verify climate-pair-pacific`

**Credits.** Graham Watt, the brief (CO₂, SST, ENSO, PDO and storms; rising, moody without being overly dark), the choice of records, listening and direction; Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding agent), music theory, mapping and all of the code; Instruments, VSCO 2 Community Edition (Versilian Studios, CC0), plus synthesizers.

**Changelog.**

- v2.0 (2026-09-25): First published version. The Kettle River replaced the Granby as the valley link (the Granby record has a 1958-66 gap); West Pacific typhoons (IBTrACS) and ocean heat content (IAP) were added; storm levels rebalanced so the rise is heard.
- v1.0 (2026-09-25): First render, not published.

- Sunspot number (SILSO; fetched, not redistributed)

|---|---|---|---|

| Cellos | global ocean surface temperature anomaly (NOAA NCEI) | chord tones, from one voice to three, louder as it warms | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Contrabass | ocean heat content, 0-2000 m (IAP v4.2) | the deep ocean filling: root, then root and fifth, louder | <span class="src R">R</span> |

| Drums | Atlantic hurricanes (HURDAT2) | tropical storm: bass-drum rub; hurricane: timpani; major: timpani, bass drum and sub; category 5: tam-tam; landfall: cymbal | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| Rumble | season's accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) | a low storm rumble | <span class="src D">D</span> |

Every step from record to sound, with its bounds: [the mapping dictionary](dictionary/climate-pair-atlantic-mapping.html) (tables in `tracks/mapping/climate-pair-atlantic/`).

**Harmony.** Key of A, one bar per year (68 bars of 7 seconds, about 8 minutes); the four beats are the seasons and the twelve pulses the months. ENSO sets the chords and the ocean's multidecadal phase sets the mode.

**Be careful about.**

- Early storms are undercounted, before routine satellite coverage (about 1966; later in the Northeast Pacific).
- Records end at different times; the AMO stopped updating in January 2023, and the piece holds its last value to the end. Interior gaps are interpolated.
- The ocean phases are 3-year means, so their turns sound about two years late.
- The volcanic cooling shape, the ENSO-to-chord table and every loudness curve are interpretive choices, not measurements.

# Meridian Chorus

Thirteen voices on the 100th meridian west, pole to pole, singing one year of daylight, air, sea and ice. [The album's page](meridian.qmd).

## Meridian Chorus, light, air, sea and ice {#meridian-layer2-wide-long}

**v0.1** · 2023-24 (solstice to solstice, 2023-12-22 to 2024-12-21) · [listen](meridian.qmd?piece=meridian_ds2023__layer2-wide-long)

*What does one year sound like along a single line of longitude, from pole to pole, when daylight, air, sea and ice each have a voice?*

**Place.** The 100th meridian west, thirteen voices one every 15 degrees from the North Pole to the South Pole, across land, ocean and ice.

**Territory.** The land and ice voices stand on Inuit Nunangat, at the Nunavut-Manitoba boundary, in South Dakota, on the Edwards Plateau in Texas, and in Antarctica. Acknowledgements are being prepared and are not yet on the page.

**Records.**

- Daylight and twilight, computed from solar geometry (solar.py)
- Daily maximum and minimum 2 m air temperature (ERA5 via Open-Meteo, CC BY 4.0)
- Sea surface temperature (NOAA OISST v2.1)
- Sea-ice concentration (NOAA/NSIDC Climate Data Record)

| Layer | Data | What you hear | |
|---|---|---|---|
| light | sun above the horizon and through civil twilight | the sung voice, on the voice's pitch; it opens from oo to ah as the sun climbs | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| air | daily maximum air temperature | the organ's registration: cold is one dark rank, warm adds the octave and opens the tone | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| night air | daily minimum air temperature | the in-breath: a warm night adds a lower, fuller band | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| sea | sea surface temperature at the ocean voices | contrabass and cello on a floor below the chorus, D1 to A3, day and night | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| ice | sea-ice concentration at the four polar voices | a lid on the sea voice and a high glass shimmer | <span class="src R">R</span> |

Every step from record to sound, with its bounds: [the mapping dictionary](dictionary/meridian-layer2-wide-long-mapping.html) (tables in `tracks/mapping/meridian-layer2-wide-long/`).

**Harmony.** D major pentatonic on thirteen distinct notes, D4 to A6 for the sky choir and D1 to A3 for the sea, so no two voices share a pitch. North sings on the left and south on the right. Three days per breath (about 16 minutes), in four movements; every voice centres on the same solar noon, so the chorus breathes together.

**Be careful about.**

- Air temperature is reanalysis at one point per voice, not a station.
- Each breath plays the mean over its block of days.
- The ear hears the season's shape, not the value at any one parallel.

**Reproduce.** `python scripts/meridian.py --variant layer2-wide-long` · seed 2023 · locked 2026-09-28 · SHA-256 of the MP3 on this site `4cddbaa4110b7f0f…` · check it with `python scripts/renders.py verify meridian-chorus-layer2:wide-long`

**Credits.** Graham Watt, the question, the meridian, listening and direction; Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding agent), mapping, sound design and all of the code; Instruments, VSCO 2 Community Edition (Versilian Studios, CC0); the sung voices are synthesized.

**Lineage.** remix of meridian-daylight.

**Changelog.**

- v0.1 (2026-09-28): First published version (layer 2.1: sea on its own floor, by hemisphere).

## Meridian Chorus, daylight {#meridian-daylight}

**v0.2** · 2023-24 (solstice to solstice, 2023-12-22 to 2024-12-21) · [listen](meridian.qmd?piece=meridian_ds2023)

*What does a year of daylight sound like along one meridian, when every voice's note lasts as long as its day?*

**Place.** The 100th meridian west, thirteen voices one every 15 degrees from pole to pole.

**Territory.** See the Meridian Chorus card; acknowledgements are being prepared.

**Records.**

- Daylight and twilight, computed from solar geometry (solar.py); no measured records

| Layer | Data | What you hear | |
|---|---|---|---|
| note | sun above -0.833° (sunrise to sunset) | organ, strings and sung voice on the voice's pitch | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| twilight | sun between -6° and -0.833° | the note swells in and fades out | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| vowel | the sun's altitude | the sung voice opens from oo to ah | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| in-breath | sun below the horizon | a faint filtered-noise inhale, peaking at midnight | <span class="src D">D</span> |

Every step from record to sound, with its bounds: [the mapping dictionary](dictionary/meridian-daylight-mapping.html) (tables in `tracks/mapping/meridian-daylight/`).

**Harmony.** D major pentatonic, D at both poles and the equator, north above and south below, D2 to D6. A week per 8-second breath (about 7 minutes). At the equinoxes every voice is about twelve hours long; at the solstices one pole holds its note through the whole breath while the other only breathes.

**Be careful about.**

- Everything is computed from solar geometry; nothing is measured.
- Refraction is a standard constant; local horizons and weather are ignored.

**Reproduce.** `python scripts/meridian.py` · seed 2023 · locked 2026-09-28 · SHA-256 of the MP3 on this site `1431374a3ae741e3…` · check it with `python scripts/renders.py verify meridian-chorus-daylight`

**Credits.** Graham Watt, the question, the meridian, listening and direction; Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding agent), mapping, sound design and all of the code; Instruments, VSCO 2 Community Edition (Versilian Studios, CC0); the sung voices are synthesized.

**Lineage.** variants: `long`, `layer2-wide-long`.

**Changelog.**

- v0.2 (2026-09-27): After a blind two-model review: an even daytime level at every latitude, the pentatonic chord restored, the poles' breathing fixed. Re-locked 2026-09-28 with unchanged audio.
- v0.1 (2026-09-27): First render.

# Superior Ice Year

One winter of ice on Lake Superior, 2025-26, heard region by region from west to east. [The album's page](superior-ice.qmd).

## Superior Ice Year {#superior-ice}

**v1.0** · 2025-26 (ice season, 2025-11-01 to 2026-06-15) · [listen](superior-ice.qmd?piece=icecover_sup2526__v1)

*How does one winter of ice move across Lake Superior, region by region, and how does it compare with the lake's recent ordinary year?*

**Place.** Lake Superior (Gichigami), cut into eight regions from the Western Arm to Whitefish Bay.

**Territory.** Anishinaabe territory, including Ojibwe nations with treaty rights there: the Robinson-Superior Treaty of 1850, and the treaties of 1836, 1842 and 1854. The acknowledgement on the piece's page is a draft, open to correction.

**Records.**

- Ice concentration, daily by region (NOAA GLERL and CoastWatch Great Lakes Node, GLSEA with NIC ice charts)
- Surface water temperature, daily by region (NOAA CoastWatch ACSPO GLSEA)
- Lake-average ice, 2008-2025 median (NOAA GLERL)
- Air temperature, wind, precipitation, snowfall and shortwave radiation (ERA5 via Open-Meteo, CC BY 4.0)

| Layer | Data | What you hear | |
|---|---|---|---|
| ice | region ice concentration | a bowed-glass tone per region, D5 to F#6 west to east, louder as the ice thickens | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| events | 3-day-smoothed daily change in region ice | freeze: a glass ping; breakup: a low drop and crack, each at a random distance (quieter, darker, later, wetter) | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| water | region surface temperature | four low string voices | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| turnover | lake-mean skin temperature crossing 4 °C | a soft sub drop | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| air | lake-mean air temperature | an organ that adds ranks and brightens as it warms | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| sun | day length at 47.6° N and shortwave radiation | a choir that swells and opens from oo to ah | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| wind | peak wind of the eight regions | a filtered-noise bed gated by gales | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| snow | region snowfall | dry unpitched ticks | <span class="src R">R</span> |
| rain | region liquid precipitation | soft harp drops | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| birds | timing from ice-off and warmth | loon and goose recordings | <span class="src S">S</span> |
| ghost | 2008-2025 median lake ice | a quiet detuned glass tone; after the data end it holds a low floor and fades (a symbolic coda), and a soft pulse marks the last day of data | <span class="src D">D</span> |
| deep water | deep water near 4 °C under the ice (known physics, not measured here) | a constant low hum | <span class="src D">D</span> |

Every step from record to sound, with its bounds: [the mapping dictionary](dictionary/superior-ice-mapping.html) (tables in `tracks/mapping/superior-ice/`).

**Harmony.** D major pentatonic. Each region is a note, low in the west and high in the east, panned by longitude, so the chord sounding at any moment is the ice pattern on the map. Three seconds per day (11 min 46 s), cut into four movements at ice-defined days: freeze-up, ice-in, long melt, open water. Higher regions are trimmed 0.5 dB a step so the east doesn't sound louder.

**Simulated, not observed.**

- Bird timing is symbolic, from each region's ice-off and warmth; the calls are recordings, not observations.
- The ghost's coda after the last day of data is symbolic.

**Be careful about.**

- Regions are wedges by distance from eight anchor points, not basins or depth zones.
- Water temperature is the satellite skin of the top millimetres, not the lake at depth.
- Air, wind and precipitation are ERA5 reanalysis at one point per region, not station observations.
- Freeze and breakup events are derived with fixed thresholds (4 points a day, 3 days apart).
- The ear does not read the map (a listening probe agreed); the page's picture carries space.

**Reproduce.** `python scripts/icecover.py --variant v1` · seed 2026 · locked 2026-09-29 · SHA-256 of the MP3 on this site `837c4a520d286b39…` · check it with `python scripts/renders.py verify icecover-superior-ice:v1`
